pages.text: Throughout the paper, $q$ denotes a prime power and $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ the finite field with $q$ elements. For a positive integer $n$ , we denote by $\Mat_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ the space of $n\times n$ matrices with entries in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ . For a given matrix $M\in\Mat_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ , we denote by $\textnormal{colsp}(M)$ the subspace of $\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$ spanned by the columns of $M$ and by $\textnormal{rowsp}(M)$ the subspace of $\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$ spanned by the rows of $M$ . We denote by $O$ the $n\times n$ zero-matrix. The standard basis vector of $\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$ is denoted by $\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}\}$ .

Definition 2.1. A matrix $A\in\Mat_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ is said to be alternating or skew-symmetric if $A=-A^{\top}$ and $A_{i,i}=0$ for all $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ . We denote by $\Alt_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ the space of $n\times n$ alternating matrices with entries in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ .

Notice that alternating matrices have always even rank, hence we have that the minimum distance of an alternating code is always even and we usually assume that it is $2d$ , for some positive integer $d$ . We use $A_{q}(n,2d)$ to denote the maximal cardinality of an alternating code in $\Alt_{n}(q)$ with the property that any two distinct codewords are at distance at least $2d$ from each other.

pages.text: Throughout this article, all graphs are assumed to be finite, undirected and without loops or multiple edges. The vertices of a graph $G$ are denoted by $V(G)$ and its edges by $E(G)$ . We also assume that $\mathbb{F}$ denotes an arbitrary field. Following the notation in [8], we denote by $\mathcal{M}_{\mathbb{F}}(G)$ the set of all matrices $M$ over $\mathbb{F}$ with rows and columns indexed by $V(G)$ , so that for every two distinct vertices $u,v\in V(G)$ , the $(u,v)-$ entry of $M$ is non-zero if and only if $\{u,v\}\in E(G)$ . Notice that the diagonal entries are allowed to be non-zero. A matrix $M$ over $\mathbb{F}$ is said to be acyclic if $M\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathbb{F}}(F)$ for a forest $F$ . If the forest $F$ is a tree, then $M$ is said to be tree-patterned.
Given a graph $G$ , the adjacency matrix of $G$ , denoted by $A(G)$ , is a $(0,1)-$ matrix in $\mathcal{M}_{\mathbb{F}}(G)$ with zero diagonal.

Let $\mathcal{M}_{\mathbb{F},0}(G)$ be the set of matrices in $\mathcal{M}_{\mathbb{F}}(G)$ with zero in the diagonal. In Section 2 we show that given a forest $F$ , the null space of any matrix in $\mathcal{M}_{\mathbb{F},0}(F)$ can be obtained by multiplying the null space of $F$ by a suitable non-singular diagonal matrix. This will allow the use of all the tools developed in [5, 6] for the study of the null space of said matrices. In particular we use the results of [6] to give an optimal time algorithm for finding a sparsest basis of the null space of the matrix. In Section 3 we prove that the rank of any matrix in $\mathcal{M}_{\mathbb{F},0}(F)$ can be found by multiplying the rank of $F$ by a suitable non-singular diagonal matrix.
Corollary 10. If $F$ is a forest and $M\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathbb{F},0}(F)$ , then $\dim{\operatorname{\mathpzc{Rank}}(M)}=2m$ , where $m$ is the size of a maximum matching in $F$ .

pages.text: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be an $[n,k,d]_{q}$ linear code. Assume that the encoding of ${\bf x}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k}$ is by the vector $\mathcal{C}({\bf x})=({\bf c}_{1}\cdot{\bf x},{\bf c}_{2}\cdot{\bf x},\ldots,{\bf c}_{n}\cdot{\bf x})\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}.$ (3) Thus the code $\mathcal{C}$ is specified by the set of $n$ points $C=\{{\bf c}_{1},\ldots,{\bf c}_{n}\}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k}$ . The set of points must have full rank for $\mathcal{C}$ to have $k$ information symbols. It is well known that the distance property is captured by the following condition (e.g., [9, theorem 1.1.6]).

Definition 2. For ${\bf c}_{i}\in C$ , we define $\loc({\bf c}_{i})$ to be the smallest integer $r$ for which there exists $R\subseteq C$ of cardinality $r$ such that ${\bf c}_{i}=\sum_{j\in R}\lambda_{j}{\bf c}_{j}.$ We further define $\loc(\mathcal{C})=\max_{i\in[n]}\loc({\bf c}_{i})$ .
Definition 3. We say that a code $\mathcal{C}$ has information locality $r$ if there exists $I\subseteq C$ of full rank such that $\loc({\bf c})\leqslant r$ for all ${\bf c}\in I.$
Theorem 5. For any $[n,k,d]_{q}$ linear code with information locality $r$ , $n-k\geqslant\left\lceil\frac{k}{r}\right\rceil+d-2.$ (5)

pages.text: A graph $G$ is $k$ -critical if $G$ is not $(k-1)$ -colorable, but every proper subgraph of $G$ is $(k-1)$ -colorable. Then every $k$ -critical graph has chromatic number $k$ and every $k$ -chromatic graph contains a $k$ -critical subgraph. The importance of the notion of criticality is that problems for $k$ -chromatic graphs may often be reduced to problems for $k$ -critical graphs, whose structure is more restricted. For example, every $k$ -critical graph is $2$ -connected and $(k-1)$ -edge-connected.

The only $1$ -critical graph is $K_{1}$ , and the only $2$ -critical graph is $K_{2}$ . The only $3$ -critical graphs are the odd cycles. For every $k\geq 4$ and every $n\geq k+2$ , there exists a $k$ -critical $n$ -vertex graph. Let $f_{k}(n)$ be the minimum number of edges in a $k$ -critical graph with $n$ vertices. Since $\delta(G)\geq k-1$ for every $k$ -critical $n$ -vertex graph $G$ , $f_{k}(n)\geq\frac{k-1}{2}n$ (1) for all $n\geq k$ , $n\neq k+1$ . Equality is achieved for $n=k$ and for $k=3$ and $n$ odd. Brooks’ Theorem [3] implies that for $k\geq 4$ and $n\geq k+2$ , the inequality in (1) is strict. In 1957, Dirac [8] asked to determine $f_{k}(n)$ and proved that for $k\geq 4$ and $n\geq k+2$ , $f_{k}(n)\geq\frac{k-1}{2}n+\frac{k-3}{2}.$ (2) The result is tight for $n=2k-1$ and yields $f_{k}(2k-1)=k^{2}-k-1$ . Dirac used his bound to evaluate chromatic number of graphs embedded into fixed surfaces. Later, Kostochka and Stiebitz [19] improved (2) to $f_{k}(n)\geq\frac{k-1}{2}n+k-3$ (3) when $n\neq 2k-1,k$ . This yields $f_{k}(2k)=k^{2}-3$ and $f_{k}(3k-2)=\frac{3k(k-1)}{2}-2$ . In his fundamental papers [11, 12], Gallai found exact values of $f_{k}(n)$ for $k+2\leq n\leq 2k-1$ :

Theorem 3 If $k\geq 4$ and $G$ is $k$ -critical, then $|E(G)|\geq\left\lceil\frac{(k+1)(k-2)|V(G)|-k(k-3)}{2(k-1)}\right\rceil$ . In other words, if $k\geq 4$ and $n\geq k,\,n\neq k+1$ , then $f_{k}(n)\geq F(k,n):=\left\lceil\frac{(k+1)(k-2)n-k(k-3)}{2(k-1)}\right\rceil.$ (9)

pages.text: Our focus will be studying a sequence that was introduced by Butler et al. [4] as a refinement of the pr-sequence of an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix $B$ over a field $\mathbb{F}$ , which they called the enhanced principal rank characteristic sequence (abbreviated epr-sequence), and which was defined as $\operatorname{epr}(B)=\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\cdots\ell_{n}$ , where $\ell_{k}=\begin{cases}\tt{A}&\text{if all the principal minors of order $k$ are nonzero;}\\ \tt{S}&\text{if some but not all the principal minors of order $k$ are nonzero;}\\ \tt{N}&\text{if none of the principal minors of order $k$ are nonzero, i.e., all are zero.}\end{cases}$ Motivated by Theorem 1.1, we focus on fields of characteristic $2$ . Although epr-sequences have received attention after their introduction in [4] (see [5], [6] and [10], for example), very little is known about epr-sequences of symmetric matrices over a field of characteristic $2$ , since the vast majority of what has appeared on the literature regarding epr-sequences has been focused on fields of characteristic not $2$ (see [6] for results on real skew-symmetric matrices). The main objective of this paper is a complete characterization of the epr-sequences that are attainable by a symmetric matrix over a field of characteristic $2$ (see Theorems 3.2, 3.9 and 3.13). We find that the attainable epr-sequences over a field of characteristic $2$ possess very special structures, which is in contrast to the family of attainable epr-sequences over a field of characteristic $0$ : for example, it was shown in [4, Section 4] that any epr-sequence of $\tt A$ s and $\tt S$ s that ends with an $\tt A$ is attainable over a field of characteristic $0$ , as well as any epr-sequence of $\tt A$ s and $\tt S$ s that ends with one or more consecutive $\tt N$ s. Another motivating factor for considering this problem is that it is a simplification of the principal minor assignment problem as stated in [8], which also served as motivation for the introduction of the pr-sequence in [2]. Note that epr-sequences provide more information than pr-sequences, and thus are a step closer to the principal minor assignment problem.
In what follows, $K_{n}$ denotes the complete graph on $n$ vertices, and $A(K_{n})$ denotes its adjacency matrix.

Proposition 2.2. Let $n\geq 2$ . Then, over a field of characteristic $2$ , $\operatorname{epr}(A(K_{n}))=\tt NA\overline{NA}$ when $n$ is even, and $\operatorname{epr}(A(K_{n}))=\tt NA\overline{NA}N$ when $n$ is odd.

Proof. Let $\operatorname{epr}(A(K_{n}))=\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\cdots\ell_{n}$ . Obviously, $\ell_{1}=\tt N$ . Observe that, for $2\leq q\leq n$ , every $q\times q$ principal submatrix of $B$ is equal to $A(K_{q})$ . Since $A(K_{q})=J_{q}-I_{q}$ , $\det(A(K_{q}))=(-1)^{q-1}(q-1)=q-1$ (in characteristic $2$ ). Hence, $\ell_{q}=\tt N$ when $q$ is odd and $\ell_{q}=\tt A$ when $q$ is even. $\square$
